sections.h2: What the Recorder of Deeds does
sections.html:
The Ray County Recorder of Deeds files the paper trail of land ownership: deeds, deeds of trust, releases, affidavits, powers of attorney, plats, surveys and military discharge records. When you sell a house in Ray County, the buyer's deed and any loan payoff release end up on file at the office in Richmond.

The phone number is 816-776-4500. Land records go back to 1820. Documents since May 1963 are digital, and anything older sits in books at the office. You can come in, call or email for a copy. Copies cost $1 per page, with an extra $2 when the copy is emailed.

Recording matters under Missouri law. Until a document is deposited with the recorder, RSMo 442.400 limits its force to the signers and anyone with actual notice. A signed deed that never reaches the Recorder leaves the buyer exposed, so confirm the title company files it right after closing.

Recording a document costs $26 for page one and $3 for every page after. Budget from that posted figure when you plan closing costs. The office takes checks, cash and debit or credit cards for recordings and copies.

sections.h2: How to get a deed recorded
sections.html:
Take it to the office, mail it, or file it electronically. When mailing, enclose a self-addressed stamped envelope for the return of the original. E-recording runs through iCounty at raymo.icounty.com, and the iCounty number is 816-295-1540.

Most sellers never file anything themselves, because the title company or closing attorney sends the deed and the lender's release. Even so, a few practical steps help:

  • Check that every signature has the printed name under it, as RSMo 59.310 requires.
  • Keep type no smaller than 8 point and make the page legible enough to copy cleanly.
  • Remember that an oversized page or an added sheet for the recorder's stamp counts as an extra page.
  • Ask the closing agent for the recording date and book or document number after filing.

A quitclaim, transfer on death deed or release should be drafted by a title company or Missouri attorney before it comes to the counter.

sections.h2: Protecting your property from deed fraud
sections.html:
Owners can sign up free for a fraud alert at deedwatch.com. You get a message each time something is filed with your name on it. If you get an alert for something you did not sign, call the Recorder at 816-776-4500.

The office cannot remove a recorded document from the public record without a court order signed by a judge. An owner who believes a forged deed was filed should speak with an attorney and can also report it to the Ray County Sheriff or the police department in the city involved. Signing up before you list a vacant or inherited house takes a few minutes and costs nothing. Owners who live out of town or who are settling an estate are the most likely to miss a fraudulent filing, so an alert is worth setting up for them first. Keep the confirmation email so you can show when you were notified.

sections.h2: Ray County housing and taxes in brief
sections.html:
Ray County is in northwest Missouri, in the Kansas City metro area, with Richmond as the seat and largest city. Population is about 23,398. A typical owned home is valued around $198,800, and owners occupy 77.3 percent of homes. Median gross rent is $782. Four school districts serve the county: Richmond R-XVI, Orrick R-XI, Lawson R-XIV and Hardin-Central C-2. A deed's legal description and the tax bill will show which one applies.

The assessor learns who owns a parcel from the recorded deed, and whoever owns it on January 1 gets the assessment. Residential assessment is 19 percent of true value (RSMo 137.115). A fresh valuation is set each odd-numbered year as of January 1, so 2027 is next.

For the actual bill, parcel number and levy district, contact the Ray County Assessor and Collector. The Recorder records ownership and does not collect tax. The bill is due December 31. If you sell in the fall, check the tax status before the deed is signed.

sections.h2: Getting a copy of a recorded deed
sections.html:
Ask in person, by phone or by email. Deed copies run $1 per page, plus $2 if you want it emailed. Certification costs $1 per document, which matters when a lender or court wants a stamped copy.

Plan on a short wait for anything recorded before May 1963, because those items are kept in books rather than as digital images. A copy of a plat or survey is $5. Sellers who cannot find their own deed usually need one for the legal description, and ordering it early keeps the title search moving. If a lender or court wants a certified copy, ask for certification when you order so you only make one trip or one request.

sections.h2: What else to settle before closing
sections.html:
After recording, property tax status comes next. Get the current bill and any delinquent years from the Ray County Collector. The title company can pay off tax liens or unpaid bills out of the proceeds. Recording goes smoothly only when the title is clean. Ask the title company early which of these they have already found.

  • Pull any old deed of trust that was paid but never released, since the release must be recorded too.
  • Order copies of recent deeds if the legal description looks wrong.
  • If the seller died, expect the title company to want probate paperwork on file before a deed is signed.
  • Sellers who need to close quickly on an inherited or tenant-occupied house sometimes take a cash offer, which still requires a recorded deed.

With a cash sale there is no buyer's lender, so closing can move faster. The ending is the same, though. The title company searches for liens, collects any tax owed, and sends the deed to Richmond to be recorded. Ask for the recording confirmation once it is done, and keep it with your closing papers. Questions about what a document means for your sale belong with your attorney or closing agent, since the Recorder's office files instruments and does not advise on them. When you go, carry the parcel number or the names on the deed, and ask how the office prefers to be paid.

faqs.q: What does it cost to record a deed in Ray County?
faqs.a: $26 for the first page and $3 for each added page. Plats and surveys are priced separately, and the office accepts cash, checks and cards.

faqs.q: Where is the Ray County Recorder of Deeds office?
faqs.a: It is in Richmond, the county seat. Call 816-776-4500 to confirm hours and where to mail a document before you send anything.

faqs.q: Can I record a deed electronically in Ray County?
faqs.a: Yes. E-recording is available through iCounty at raymo.icounty.com, and the iCounty contact number is 816-295-1540. Title companies commonly use it for closings.

faqs.q: How far back do Ray County land records go?
faqs.a: To 1820. Records from May 1963 forward are digital, and older items are kept in books at the Recorder's office.

faqs.q: What if someone records a deed on my property without my consent?
faqs.a: Call the Recorder at 816-776-4500 and see an attorney. The Recorder cannot remove a filed document without a court order, so a judge must act. You can also report suspected fraud to the Ray County Sheriff.
